Es un error usar esta opción con el puntero de marco o el puntero de pila. El uso de esta opción para otros registros que tienen roles fijos y omnipresentes en el modelo de ejecución de la máquina produce resultados desastrosos.

Esta opción no tiene forma negativa, ya que especifica una elección de tres vías.

-fcall-saved-reg
Trata el registro llamado reg como un registro asignable guardado por las funciones. Puede ser asignado incluso para temporales o variables que viven a través de una llamada. Las funciones compiladas de esta manera guardan y restauran el registro reg si lo utilizan.

Es un error usar esta opción con el puntero de marco o el puntero de pila. El uso de esta opción para otros registros que tienen roles fijos y omnipresentes en el modelo de ejecución de la máquina produce resultados desastrosos.

Un desastre de otro tipo resulta del uso de esta opción para un registro en el que se pueden devolver valores de función.

Esta opción no tiene forma negativa, ya que especifica una elección de tres vías.

-fpack-struct[=n]
Sin un valor especificado, agrupa todos los miembros de la estructura sin huecos. Cuando se especifica un valor (que debe ser una pequeña potencia de dos), agrupa los miembros de la estructura según este valor, representando la alineación máxima (es decir, los objetos con requisitos de alineación predeterminados mayores que este se emiten potencialmente desalineados en la siguiente ubicación adecuada).

Advertencia: el modificador -fpack-struct hace que GCC genere código que no es binariamente compatible con el código generado sin ese modificador. Además, hace que el código sea subóptimo. Úselo para cumplir con una interfaz binaria de aplicación no predeterminada.

-fleading-underscore
Esta opción y su contraparte, -fno-leading-underscore, cambian forzosamente la forma en que los símbolos de C se representan en el archivo objeto. Un uso es ayudar a enlazar con código ensamblador obsoleto.

Advertencia: el modificador -fleading-underscore hace que GCC genere código que no es binariamente compatible con el código generado sin ese modificador. Úselo para cumplir con una interfaz binaria de aplicación no predeterminada. No todos los destinos proporcionan soporte completo para este modificador.

-ftls-model=model
Altera el modelo de almacenamiento local de hilos (TLS) que se utilizará. El argumento model debe ser uno de global-dynamic, local-dynamic, initial-exec o local-exec. Tenga en cuenta que la elección está sujeta a optimización: el compilador puede usar un modelo más eficiente para símbolos no visibles fuera de la unidad de traducción, o si no se proporciona -fpic en la línea de comandos.

El valor predeterminado sin -fpic es initial-exec; con -fpic el valor predeterminado es global-dynamic.

-ftrampolines
Para destinos que normalmente necesitan trampolines para funciones anidadas, genéralos siempre en lugar de usar descriptores. De lo contrario, para destinos que no los necesitan, como por ejemplo HP-PA o IA-64, no haga nada.

Un trampolín es un pequeño fragmento de código que se crea en tiempo de ejecución en la pila cuando se toma la dirección de una función anidada, y se utiliza para llamar a la función anidada indirectamente. Por lo tanto, requiere que la pila sea ejecutable para que el programa funcione correctamente.

-fno-trampolines está habilitado por defecto en una base lenguaje por lenguaje para permitir que el compilador evite generarlos, si calcula que esto es seguro, y reemplazarlos con descriptores. Los descriptores están formados solo por datos, pero el código generado debe estar preparado para tratarlos. A fecha de hoy, -fno-trampolines está habilitado por defecto solo para Ada.

Además, el código compilado con -ftrampolines y el código compilado con -fno-trampolines no son binariamente compatibles si hay funciones anidadas presentes. Por lo tanto, esta opción debe usarse en todo el programa y manipularse con extremo cuidado.

Para lenguajes distintos de Ada, las opciones "-ftrampolines" y "-fno-trampolines" actualmente no tienen efecto, y los trampolines se generan siempre en plataformas que los necesitan para funciones anidadas.

-ftrampoline-impl=[stack|heap]
Por defecto, los trampolines se generan en la pila. Sin embargo, ciertas plataformas (como el Apple M1) no permiten una pila ejecutable. Compilar con -ftrampoline-impl=heap genera llamadas a "__gcc_nested_func_ptr_created" y "__gcc_func_ptr_deleted" para asignar y liberar espacio de trampolín en el heap ejecutable. Estas funciones se implementan en libgcc y solo se proporcionarán en destinos específicos: x86_64 Darwin, x86_64 y aarch64 Linux. TENGA EN CUENTA: No se garantiza que los trampolines del heap se liberen correctamente si usa "setjmp", instancia funciones anidadas y luego "longjmp" a un estado anterior a la asignación de dichas funciones anidadas.
-fvisibility=[default|internal|hidden|protected]
Establece la visibilidad predeterminada de los símbolos de la imagen ELF a la opción especificada: todos los símbolos se marcan con esta opción a menos que se anule en el código. El uso de esta función puede mejorar sustancialmente los tiempos de enlace y carga de las bibliotecas de objetos compartidos, producir código más optimizado, proporcionar una exportación de API casi perfecta y prevenir conflictos de símbolos. Se recomienda encarecidamente que lo utilice en cualquier objeto compartido que distribuya.

A pesar de la nomenclatura, default siempre significa público; es decir, disponible para enlazar desde fuera del objeto compartido. protected e internal son bastante inútiles en el uso práctico, por lo que la única otra opción comúnmente utilizada es hidden. El valor predeterminado si no se especifica -fvisibility es default, es decir, hacer que todos los símbolos sean públicos.

Una buena explicación de los beneficios de garantizar que los símbolos ELF tengan la visibilidad correcta se ofrece en "How To Write Shared Libraries" de Ulrich Drepper (que se puede encontrar en https://www.akkadia.org/drepper/), sin embargo, una solución superior posible gracias a esta opción para marcar elementos como ocultos cuando el valor predeterminado es público es hacer que el valor predeterminado sea oculto y marcar los elementos como públicos. Esta es la norma con las DLL en Windows y con -fvisibility=hidden y "__attribute__ ((visibility("default")))" en lugar de "__declspec(dllexport)" se obtiene una semántica casi idéntica con sintaxis idéntica. Esto es una gran ayuda para quienes trabajan con proyectos multiplataforma.

Para quienes añaden soporte de visibilidad a código existente, puede encontrar útil "#pragma GCC visibility". Esto funciona encerrando las declaraciones cuya visibilidad desea establecer con (por ejemplo) "#pragma GCC visibility push(hidden)" y "#pragma GCC visibility pop". Tenga en cuenta que la visibilidad de los símbolos debe considerarse parte del contrato de la interfaz API y, por lo tanto, todo el código nuevo siempre debe especificar la visibilidad cuando no sea la predeterminada; es decir, las declaraciones solo para uso dentro del DSO local deben siempre marcarse explícitamente como ocultas para evitar sobrecargas de indirección PLT, lo que hace que esto sea muy claro también ayuda a la legibilidad y la autodescripción del código. Tenga en cuenta que debido a los requisitos de la especificación ISO C++, "operator new" y "operator delete" siempre deben ser de visibilidad predeterminada.

Tenga en cuenta que las cabeceras de fuera de su proyecto, en particular las cabeceras del sistema y las cabeceras de cualquier otra biblioteca que utilice, pueden no esperar ser compiladas con una visibilidad diferente a la predeterminada. Es posible que necesite decir explícitamente "#pragma GCC visibility push(default)" antes de incluir dichas cabeceras.

"extern" las declaraciones no se ven afectadas por -fvisibility, por lo que mucho código se puede recompilar con -fvisibility=hidden sin modificaciones. Sin embargo, esto significa que las llamadas a funciones "extern" sin visibilidad explícita utilizan el PLT, por lo que es más efectivo usar "__attribute ((visibility))" y/o "#pragma GCC visibility" para indicar al compilador qué declaraciones "extern" deben tratarse como ocultas.

Tenga en cuenta que -fvisibility afecta a las entidades de enlace vago de C++. Esto significa que, por ejemplo, una clase de excepción que se lanza entre DSOs debe marcarse explícitamente con visibilidad predeterminada para que los nodos type_info se unifiquen entre los DSOs.

Una descripción general de estas técnicas, sus beneficios y cómo usarlas se encuentra en https://gcc.gnu.org/wiki/Visibility.

-fstrict-volatile-bitfields
Esta opción debe usarse si los accesos a campos de bits volátiles (u otros campos de estructura, aunque el compilador generalmente respeta esos tipos de todos modos) deben usar un solo acceso del ancho del tipo del campo, alineado a una alineación natural si es posible. Por ej

Options Controlling Code Generation

This section describes the compiler flags that control aspects of code generation. This includes options such as those controlling optimization levels, instruction scheduling, and the generation of debugging information.

-falign-functions
=number
-fno-align-functions
Align the starting address of each function to the given number byte boundary. No function is aligned if "-fno-align-functions" is specified. The default value for this option is determined by the target architecture.
-falign-loops
=number
-fno-align-loops
Align the starting address of each loop for the given number byte boundary. Not all loops are aligned if "-fno-align-loops" is specified. The loop alignment is implemented by the instruction scheduler. The default value for this option is determined by the target architecture.
-falign-labels
=number
-fno-align-labels
Align the address of any label to the given number byte boundary. Not all labels are aligned if "-fno-align-labels" is specified. The default value for this option is determined by the target architecture.
-falign-jumps
=number
-fno-align-jumps
Align the address of any jump instruction to the given number byte boundary. Not all jump instructions are aligned if "-fno-align-jumps" is specified. The default value for this option is determined by the target architecture.
-fno-align-branch-prob
When aligning branches, don't use profilng information to align them. When this option is enabled, the compiler aligns branches based on profiling information collected by the "gprof" utility. The default behavior is to use profilng information.
-fallow-string-ops
-fno-allow-string-ops
When this option is enabled, the compiler is allowed to use string operations for memory copies. The default is to use string operations. This option is useful if the target architecture does not have any string operations, or if they are inefficient. For example, some embedded systems may not have string operations.
-fargument-alias
-fno-argument-alias
This option tells the compiler that arguments to functions may alias each other. When this option is enabled, the compiler must assume that arguments to functions may alias each other. This is the default behavior. When disabled, the compiler may, under certain circumstances, make assumptions about argument aliasing that can improve performance. This option is primarily intended for use with languages that do not support pointer aliasing, such as FORTRAN. C and C++ allow pointer aliasing, so use this option with caution.
-fassociative-math
-fno-associative-math
This option tells the compiler that it can assume that the associative property of floating-point arithmetic holds, i.e. (a+b)+c = a+(b+c), and (a*b)*c = a*(b*c). This option can enable optimizations that might not be valid under the C and C++ arithmetic rules. The default is to not assume the associative property holds.
-fbitwise-ops
-fno-bitwise-ops
This option controls whether the compiler is allowed to perform bitwise operations on integers. When this option is enabled, the compiler may use bitwise operations to implement integer arithmetic. This can lead to more efficient code. When disabled, the compiler must use standard arithmetic operations. The default is to use bitwise operations.
-fbranch-probabilities
-fno-branch-probabilities
This option enables the compiler to use profiling information to optimize branches. When this option is enabled, the compiler gathers profiling information during a previous run of the program and uses it to make optimizations. When disabled, the compiler does not use profiling information. The default is to use profiling information.
-fbranch-target-inlining
-fno-branch-target-inlining
This option enables the compiler to inline functions that are called frequently. When this option is enabled, the compiler identifies frequently called functions and inlines them at the call site. This can improve performance by reducing function call overhead. The default is to inline frequently called functions.
-fcaller-saves
-fno-caller-saves
This option tells the compiler that it can save caller-saved registers before calling a function. Caller-saved registers are registers that the caller must preserve across a function call. When this option is enabled, the compiler can save these registers before calling a function and restore them afterwards. This can improve performance by allowing the compiler to use more registers for local variables. The default is to save caller-saved registers.
-fcse-follow-jump
-fno-cse-follow-jump
This option tells the compiler to follow jumps when performing common subexpression elimination. When this option is enabled, the compiler will attempt to eliminate common subexpressions even if they are separated by a jump. This can improve performance by reducing redundant computations. The default is to follow jumps.
-fcse-skip-blocks
-fno-cse-skip-blocks
This option tells the compiler to skip blocks when performing common subexpression elimination. When this option is enabled, the compiler will skip blocks that do not contain any common subexpressions. This can improve performance by reducing the amount of code that needs to be analyzed. The default is to skip blocks.
-fdata-sections
-fno-data-sections
Place each data item in its own section in the output file. This can allow the linker to optimize the program by placing related data items together. It may also allow unused portions of data to be removed. This option is disabled by default.
-fdefault-integer-8
-fno-default-integer-8
Use 8-bit integers by default instead of 32-bit integers. This can save memory and improve performance on some architectures. This option is enabled by default.
-fdelayed-branch
-fno-delayed-branch
Enable or disable the issue of delayed branches. This is useful for the processor which supports delayed branches. This option is enabled by default.
-fdefer-pop
-fno-defer-pop
For each function, the compiler delays popping of the stack frame until the end of the function. This can improve performance on some architectures by allowing the compiler to reuse the space freed by register spills. This option is enabled by default.
-fexplicit-zero-in-data
-fno-explicit-zero-in-data
This option specifies whether the compiler should emit explicit zeros for all zero-valued data items. This option is enabled by default. If disabled, the compiler may omit explicit zeros for zero-valued data items, which can reduce the size of the executable file.
Do not use register R for any purpose. The register cannot be used for any variable or temporary quantities. The compiler's goal is to prevent the register from being used.

For example, if you have a special register R which is used for calls to operating system routines, you can use "-ffixed-R" to prevent the compiler from using the register.

This option conflicts with "-ffixed-range=a..b".

The register name R must be a valid register name for the target architecture.

Do not confuse "-ffixed-" with "-fcall-saved". In particular, "-ffixed-" disables the use of the register in any context, while "-fcall-saved" only affects the use of the register as part of the calling convention.

This option is usually not needed unless you are writing a compiler support library or are integrating GCC with another compiler.

There is no corresponding enable option. The default is to not reserve any registers.

This option conflicts with "-ffixed-range=a..b".

The register name R must be a valid register name for the target architecture.

Do not confuse "-ffixed-" with "-fcall-saved". In particular, "-ffixed-" disables the use of the register in any context, while "-fcall-saved" only affects the use of the register as part of the calling convention.

This option is usually not needed unless you are writing a compiler support library or are integrating GCC with another compiler.

There is no corresponding enable option. The default is to not reserve any registers.

-ffixed-range=a..b
Do not use registers a through b for any purpose. The registers cannot be used for any variable or temporary quantities. The compiler's goal is to prevent the registers from being used.

For example, on some 64-bit targets, the following command avoids using the lower 16 registers:

gcc -ffixed-range=r0..r15 target.c

This option conflicts with "-ffixed-".

The register names a and b must be valid register names for the target architecture. The register range is inclusive.

Do not confuse "-ffixed-range=a..b" with "-fcall-saved-range=a..b". In particular, "-ffixed-range=a..b" disables the use of the registers in any context, while "-fcall-saved-range=a..b" only affects the use of the registers as part of the calling convention.

This option is usually not needed unless you are writing a compiler support library or are integrating GCC with another compiler.

There is no corresponding enable option. The default is to not reserve any registers.

-ffloat-store
-fno-float-store
Prevent the reordering of floating point load and store operations. This can be useful when working with hardware that does not support out-of-order memory access, or when dealing with memory-mapped floating-point registers. This option is enabled by default.
-fforce-indirect-call
-fno-force-indirect-call
Force the use of indirect calls for all function calls. This can be useful for debugging or for implementing dynamic dispatch mechanisms. This option is disabled by default.
-ffp-contract=STYLE
-fno-fp-contract
STYLE may be off, on or fast.

"-ffp-contract=off" disables expression fusion of floating-point operations (where the result of one expression is used as an operand to another, such as "a=b+c; d=a+e;").

"-ffp-contract=on" enables expression fusion of floating-point operations. This is the default behavior.

"-ffp-contract=fast" enables expression fusion of floating-point operations and allows intermediate results to be used in expression fusion even if they are not the exact result of the expression.

-fguess-long-jumps
-fno-guess-long-jumps
Assume that a jump is too long to be used by a branch instruction. This can improve performance by avoiding unnecessary branch instructions. This option is enabled by default.
-fimplicit-online-calls
-fno-implicit-online-calls
This option instructs the compiler to assume that all calls to functions declared with the "inline" keyword are inlined. This can improve performance by reducing function call overhead. The default is to not assume inlining.
-finline-functions
-fno-inline-functions
This option enables or disables the inlining of functions. When enabled, the compiler attempts to inline functions at call sites to reduce function call overhead. The default behavior is to inline functions.
-finstrument-functions
-fno-instrument-functions
This option enables or disables the insertion of instrumentation calls before and after each function call. When enabled, the compiler inserts calls to "__cyg_profile_func_enter" and "__cyg_profile_func_exit" before and after each function call, respectively. This can be used for profiling or other code analysis purposes. The default behavior is to not insert instrumentation calls.
-finstrument-functions-exclude-file=FILENAME
Set this to the name of a file listing function names, one per line. The compiler skips the instrumentation calls for any functions listed in this file. This option is useful for excluding certain functions, such as performance-critical ones or library functions, from instrumentation. This option is disabled by default.
-finstrument-functions-exclude-dir=DIRNAME
Set this to the name of a directory. The compiler skips the instrumentation calls for any functions defined in source files located within this directory. This option is useful for excluding entire directories of source files from instrumentation. This option is disabled by default.
-fira-loop-pressure
-fno-ira-loop-pressure
This option enables or disables the consideration of loop pressure in the Iterated Register Allocation (IRA) pass. Loop pressure refers to the number of registers used within a loop. When enabled, IRA takes loop pressure into account to make more informed register allocation decisions, potentially improving performance in loops. The default behavior is to consider loop pressure.
-fjump-table-max-entries=NUMBER
This option specifies the maximum number of entries a jump table may have. If a switch statement has more entries than this number, the compiler generates a jump table. Otherwise, it generates a jump table. The default value is 0, which means that jump tables are always generated. This can be useful for optimizing code size by avoiding jump tables for small switch statements.
-fkeep-inline-functions
-fno-keep-inline-functions
This option instructs the compiler to keep all inline functions, even if they are not used. This can be useful for debugging or for creating libraries where inline functions might be used by other modules. The default behavior is to discard unused inline functions.
-flive-record-data
-fno-live-record-data
This option enables or disables the recording of live variable data. When enabled, the compiler records live variable data, which can be used for debugging or analysis purposes. The default behavior is to not record live variable data.
-flive-patching
-fno-live-patching
This option enables or disables live patching. Live patching allows you to modify code at runtime without stopping the program. This can be useful for updating critical systems or for debugging in production environments. The default behavior is to disable live patching.
-flocal-ivars
-fno-local-ivars
This option tells the compiler to treat instance variables (ivars) as local variables when possible. This can improve performance by allowing the compiler to make more aggressive optimizations. The default behavior is to not treat ivars as local variables.
-flong-jumps
-fno-long-jumps
This option enables or disables the generation of long jump instructions. Long jumps are used to transfer control to a distant location in the code. When enabled, the compiler generates long jump instructions when necessary. The default behavior is to generate long jump instructions.
-floop-block
-fno-loop-block
This option enables or disables loop blocking. Loop blocking is an optimization technique that divides loops into smaller blocks to improve cache performance. When enabled, the compiler attempts to apply loop blocking. The default behavior is to apply loop blocking.
-floop-distribution
-fno-loop-distribution
This option enables or disables loop distribution. Loop distribution is an optimization technique that splits a single loop into multiple loops, each containing a subset of the original loop's iterations. This can improve instruction-level parallelism and reduce loop overhead. The default behavior is to apply loop distribution.
-floop-invariant-control-flow
-fno-loop-invariant-control-flow
This option enables or disables the optimization of loop-invariant control flow. This optimization moves control flow statements (e.g., conditionals) that do not depend on loop variables outside the loop, reducing redundant checks within the loop. The default behavior is to perform this optimization.
-floop-optimize
-fno-loop-optimize
This option enables or disables loop optimizations. When enabled, the compiler applies various loop optimization techniques, such as loop unrolling, loop unswitching, and loop fusion, to improve performance. The default behavior is to apply loop optimizations.
-floop-parallelize
-fno-loop-parallelize
This option enables or disables loop parallelization. When enabled, the compiler attempts to identify loops that can be executed in parallel and generates parallel code using directives or intrinsic functions. The default behavior is to not parallelize loops.
-floop-pmatrix
-fno-loop-pmatrix
This option enables or disables the transformation of loops that compute matrix products into a form that is more amenable to instruction-level parallelism. When enabled, the compiler attempts to apply this transformation. The default behavior is to apply this transformation.
-floop-unroll-and-split
-fno-loop-unroll-and-split
This option enables or disables the loop unroll and split optimization. This optimization unrolls a loop and then splits the unrolled loop into multiple smaller loops, which can improve cache performance and reduce loop overhead. The default behavior is to apply this optimization.
-floop-unswitch
-fno-loop-unswitch
This option enables or disables loop unswitching. Loop unswitching moves loop-invariant conditional branches outside the loop, reducing the number of times the condition is evaluated and potentially improving performance. The default behavior is to apply loop unswitching.
-fmemin-align=N
Set the minimum alignment for memory access to N bytes. This option can be used to enforce stricter alignment requirements for memory accesses, which may be necessary for certain hardware architectures or data structures. The default value is determined by the target architecture.
-fmerge-constants
-fno-merge-constants
Merge identical constants into a single copy in the output file. This can reduce the size of the executable file. This option is enabled by default.
-fmerge-debug-info
-fno-merge-debug-info
Merge debug information for duplicate entities. This can reduce the size of the debug information, making the debug symbols smaller. This option is enabled by default.
-fmove-loop-invariants
-fno-move-loop-invariants
This option enables or disables the hoisting of loop-invariant computations out of loops. This optimization can improve performance by reducing redundant computations within loops. The default behavior is to hoist loop-invariant computations.
-fms-extensions
-fno-ms-extensions
Enable or disable Microsoft extensions to the C/C++ language. These extensions are specific to Microsoft compilers and may not be portable. The default behavior is to not enable Microsoft extensions.
-fomit-frame-pointer
-fno-omit-frame-pointer
Omit the frame pointer register when it is not needed. This can improve performance by freeing up a register for general use. However, it can make debugging more difficult. The default behavior is to omit the frame pointer when possible.
-foptimize-for-size
-fno-optimize-for-size
Optimize for code size rather than execution speed. This can result in smaller executable files, which may be important for embedded systems or when disk space is limited. The default behavior is to optimize for speed.
-fpack-struct
-fno-pack-struct
Pack structure members tightly, without padding. This can reduce the size of structures, but may also lead to performance degradation due to unaligned memory accesses. The default behavior is to not pack structures.
-fpcc-struct-return
-fno-pcc-struct-return
Return structure and union types in registers, when possible. This option is enabled by default. When disabled, structures and unions are returned on the stack.
-fpeephole
-fno-peephole
Enable or disable the peephole optimizer. The peephole optimizer performs local optimizations on a small block of code (a "peephole"). This can improve performance by eliminating redundant instructions and improving code sequences. The default behavior is to enable the peephole optimizer.
-fpeephole2
-fno-peephole2
Enable or disable the second peephole optimizer. This optimizer performs more aggressive local optimizations than the first peephole optimizer. The default behavior is to enable the second peephole optimizer.
-fpic
-fno-pic
Generate position-independent code. This is useful for shared libraries, as it allows the code to be loaded at any address in memory. The default behavior is to generate position-dependent code.
-fpic-data
-fno-pic-data
Generate position-independent data. This is useful for shared libraries that contain data that needs to be accessed relative to the code. The default behavior is to generate position-dependent data.
-fplan9-extensions
-fno-plan9-extensions
Enable or disable Plan 9 extensions to the C/C++ language. These extensions are specific to the Plan 9 operating system and may not be portable. The default behavior is to not enable Plan 9 extensions.
-fplt
-fno-plt
Enable or disable the use of the Procedure Linkage Table (PLT) for function calls. The PLT is used to resolve function calls at runtime, which can be useful for dynamic linking. However, it can introduce overhead. The default behavior is to use the PLT.
-fprefetch-loop-arrays
-fno-prefetch-loop-arrays
This option enables or disables the generation of prefetch instructions for array accesses within loops. Prefetch instructions suggest to the processor that data will be needed soon, potentially improving memory access performance. The default behavior is to generate prefetch instructions.
-fregmove
-fno-regmove
Enable or disable the optimization that moves values between registers. This can improve performance by allowing the compiler to make better use of available registers. The default behavior is to enable this optimization.
-fregparm=number
Number of registers to use for function arguments. The default value is determined by the target architecture. Using more registers can improve performance by reducing stack usage.
-freorder
-fno-reorder
Enable or disable instruction reordering. Instruction reordering rearranges instructions to improve instruction-level parallelism and hide latencies. The default behavior is to enable instruction reordering.
-fsection-anchors
-fno-section-anchors
This option enables or disables the generation of section anchors. Section anchors are markers that help the linker to place code and data sections appropriately. This can improve performance by reducing the overhead associated with indirect jumps and calls. The default behavior is to generate section anchors.
-fsegment-reachable-boot-code
-fno-segment-reachable-boot-code
This option enables or disables the segmentation of reachable boot code. This optimization is specific to certain embedded systems and may improve performance by allowing the boot code to be placed in a more accessible memory region. The default behavior is to not segment reachable boot code.
-fselective-scheduling
-fno-selective-scheduling
Enable or disable selective instruction scheduling. Selective scheduling tries to schedule instructions only when it is likely to be beneficial, reducing compile time overhead. The default behavior is to enable selective scheduling.
-fshort-enums
-fno-short-enums
This option instructs the compiler to use the smallest possible integer type for enumerations. This can reduce the size of enumerations, which may be important for memory-constrained systems. The default behavior is to use an `int` for enumerations.
-fshort-wchar
-fno-short-wchar
Use 16-bit for "wchar_t" by default. This option is enabled by default. It can be useful for systems that use UTF-16 encoding for wide characters. Note that this may cause incompatibility with systems that use UTF-32.
-fsigned-bitfields
-funsigned-bitfields
These options control whether the default bit-field type is signed or unsigned. The default is unsigned. Using signed bit-fields can be useful when dealing with signed quantities, but may lead to unexpected behavior if the sign bit is not handled correctly.
-fsigned-char
-funsigned-char
These options control whether the default character type is signed or unsigned. The default is implementation-defined. Using unsigned char can be useful when dealing with character codes that may exceed 127, while signed char may be more appropriate for representing ASCII characters.
-fsplit-loops
-fno-split-loops
This option enables or disables loop splitting. Loop splitting divides a single loop into multiple smaller loops, which can improve cache performance and reduce loop overhead. The default behavior is to apply loop splitting.
-fsplit-wide-types
-fno-split-wide-types
Split up types larger than the natural word size and emit code for them. This can improve performance on architectures where operations on large types are not efficiently supported. The default behavior is to split wide types.
-fstack-reuse
-fno-stack-reuse
This option enables or disables stack frame reuse. When enabled, the compiler attempts to reuse stack frames for nested function calls, which can reduce stack usage and improve performance. The default behavior is to reuse stack frames.
-fstack-usage
Print a table of functions called by each function and of the maximum stack usage of each function. This option is disabled by default.
-fstrict-aliasing
-fno-strict-aliasing
This option enables or disables strict aliasing rules. When enabled, the compiler assumes that pointers of different types do not alias each other. This can improve performance by allowing more aggressive optimizations. However, it may lead to incorrect behavior if pointers of different types are used to access the same memory location. The default behavior is to enable strict aliasing rules.
-fstrict-prototype
-fno-strict-prototype
This option enables or disables strict prototype checking. When enabled, the compiler generates an error if a function is called with a signature that does not exactly match its prototype. This can help to catch errors related to function call conventions. The default behavior is to enable strict prototype checking.
-fstring-str=size
Set the maximum size of string operations to size. If a string operation is larger than this size, the compiler generates a loop instead of a string operation. This option is enabled by default.
-fswdiv
-fno-swdiv
This option enables or disables the use of scaled integer division. Scaled integer division can be more efficient than standard integer division on some architectures. The default behavior is to use scaled integer division.
-fswpp
-fno-swpp
This option enables or disables the optimization of switch statements by splitting them into multiple smaller switch statements. This can improve performance by reducing the number of comparisons needed to find the correct branch. The default behavior is to apply this optimization.
-ftabstop=N
Set the distance between tab stops to N characters. This option affects the column numbering in error messages and diagnostic output. The default value is 8.
-ftarget-align
-fno-target-align
Enable or disable alignment of target addresses. This can improve performance by ensuring that data is aligned on natural boundaries. The default behavior is to align target addresses.
-fthread-jumps
-fno-thread-jumps
This option enables or disables the optimization of threading jumps. Threading jumps rearranges jump instructions to improve instruction locality and reduce branch prediction misses. The default behavior is to apply this optimization.
-ftls-model=MODEL
Assume that the thread-local storage model is MODEL. The possible models are "global-dynamic", "local-dynamic", "initial-exec" and "local-exec".

The default for this option depends on the target system.

"global-dynamic" The address of the TLS block is computed dynamically at runtime. This is the most flexible model, but also the slowest.

"local-dynamic" The address of the TLS block is computed dynamically at runtime. However, this model assumes that all threads have the same TLS block size, which can improve performance.

"initial-exec" The TLS block is allocated at program startup. This model is the fastest, but it is only available if all TLS accesses are known at compile time.

"local-exec" The TLS block is allocated at program startup. This model assumes that only one thread accesses the TLS block, which can improve performance.

-ftrapv
-fno-trapv
This option enables or disables trapping on signed integer overflow. When enabled, the compiler inserts checks for signed integer overflow and generates a trap if overflow occurs. This can help to catch bugs related to integer overflow. The default behavior is to not trap on signed integer overflow.
-ftree-bit-width=N
Set the width of integer types in the Tree representation to N bits. This option can affect the behavior of bitwise operations and integer promotions. The default value is determined by the target architecture.
-ftree-chase-for-loop
-fno-tree-chase-for-loop
This option enables or disables the optimization that transforms standard for loops into a form that is more amenable to optimizations. This can improve performance by allowing the compiler to apply more aggressive optimizations to loops. The default behavior is to apply this optimization.
-ftree-ccp
-fno-tree-ccp
Enable or disable the CCP (Constant Propagation) optimization on the intermediate representation tree. This optimization propagates constants through the code, potentially simplifying expressions and improving performance. The default behavior is to enable this optimization.
-ftree-chase-for-loop
-fno-tree-chase-for-loop
This option enables or disables the optimization that transforms standard for loops into a form that is more amenable to optimizations. This can improve performance by allowing the compiler to apply more aggressive optimizations to loops. The default behavior is to apply this optimization.
-ftree-chase-goto
-fno-tree-chase-goto
This option enables or disables the optimization that transforms goto statements into a form that is more amenable to optimizations. This can improve performance by allowing the compiler to apply more aggressive optimizations to control flow. The default behavior is to apply this optimization.
-ftree-chase-if-goto
-fno-tree-chase-if-goto
This option enables or disables the optimization that transforms if-goto statements into a form that is more amenable to optimizations. This can improve performance by allowing the compiler to apply more aggressive optimizations to control flow. The default behavior is to apply this optimization.
-ftree-chase-if-return
-fno-tree-chase-if-return
This option enables or disables the optimization that transforms if-return statements into a form that is more amenable to optimizations. This can improve performance by allowing the compiler to apply more aggressive optimizations to control flow. The default behavior is to apply this optimization.
-ftree-chase-loop
-fno-tree-chase-loop
This option enables or disables the optimization that transforms loops into a form that is more amenable to optimizations. This can improve performance by allowing the compiler to apply more aggressive optimizations to loops. The default behavior is to apply this optimization.
-ftree-chase-return
-fno-tree-chase-return
This option enables or disables the optimization that transforms return statements into a form that is more amenable to optimizations. This can improve performance by allowing the compiler to apply more aggressive optimizations to control flow. The default behavior is to apply this optimization.
-ftree-chase-switch
-fno-tree-chase-switch
This option enables or disables the optimization that transforms switch statements into a form that is more amenable to optimizations. This can improve performance by allowing the compiler to apply more aggressive optimizations to control flow. The default behavior is to apply this optimization.
-ftree-coalesce-inlines
-fno-tree-coalesce-inlines
This option enables or disables the coalescing of inline function calls in the tree representation. This optimization can reduce the overhead associated with inline function calls. The default behavior is to apply this optimization.
-ftree-copy-propagate
-fno-tree-copy-propagate
Enable or disable the copy propagation optimization on the intermediate representation tree. This optimization replaces variables with their assigned values, potentially simplifying expressions and improving performance. The default behavior is to enable this optimization.
-ftree-dce
-fno-tree-dce
Enable or disable the dead code elimination optimization on the intermediate representation tree. This optimization removes code that has no effect on the program's output, potentially improving performance and reducing code size. The default behavior is to enable this optimization.
-ftree-dominator-inlining
-fno-tree-dominator-inlining
This option enables or disables inlining based on dominator analysis. Dominator analysis helps identify code regions that are guaranteed to be executed, allowing for more aggressive inlining decisions. The default behavior is to apply this optimization.
-ftree-for-if
-fno-tree-for-if
This option enables or disables the transformation of for loops into if statements. This optimization can improve performance by allowing the compiler to apply more aggressive optimizations to loops. The default behavior is to apply this optimization.
-ftree-fre
-fno-tree-fre
Enable or disable the full redundant expression elimination optimization on the intermediate representation tree. This optimization removes redundant computations, potentially improving performance. The default behavior is to enable this optimization.
-ftree-loop-distribution
-fno-tree-loop-distribution
This option enables or disables loop distribution optimization on the intermediate representation tree. Loop distribution splits a single loop into multiple loops, which can improve instruction-level parallelism and reduce loop overhead. The default behavior is to apply this optimization.
-ftree-loop-if-convert
-fno-tree-loop-if-convert
This option enables or disables the conversion of if statements inside loops to conditional instructions. This can improve performance by reducing control flow overhead within loops. The default behavior is to apply this optimization.
-ftree-loop-load-store-extend
-fno-tree-loop-load-store-extend
This option enables or disables the optimization that extends loads and stores within loops to cover the entire loop body. This can improve performance by reducing memory access overhead. The default behavior is to apply this optimization.
-ftree-loop-vectorize
-fno-tree-loop-vectorize
This option enables or disables loop vectorization on the intermediate representation tree. Vectorization transforms loops to operate on multiple data elements simultaneously using SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) instructions, potentially improving performance significantly. The default behavior is to apply loop vectorization.
-ftree-live-range-split
-fno-tree-live-range-split
This option enables or disables the splitting of live ranges in the tree representation. This optimization can improve register allocation by breaking long live ranges into smaller ones, allowing registers to be reused more effectively. The default behavior is to apply this optimization.
-ftree-parallelize-all
-fno-tree-parallelize-all
This option enables or disables the parallelization of all loops found in the tree representation. This optimization attempts to parallelize loops using techniques like loop vectorization and loop unrolling to improve instruction-level parallelism. The default behavior is to not parallelize all loops.
-ftree-phiprop
-fno-tree-phiprop
Enable or disable the PHI-propagation optimization on the intermediate representation tree. PHI-propagation is an optimization that replaces PHI nodes (used in control flow graphs to merge values from different paths) with simpler constructs when possible. The default behavior is to enable this optimization.
-ftree-pre
-fno-tree-pre
Enable or disable the premature common subexpression elimination optimization on the intermediate representation tree. This optimization attempts to eliminate common subexpressions early in the compilation process. The default behavior is to enable this optimization.
-ftree-pta
-fno-tree-pta
Enable or disable the pointer-based type-based aliasing optimization on the intermediate representation tree. This optimization uses pointer analysis to determine potential aliasing relationships, which can improve the effectiveness of other optimizations. The default behavior is to enable this optimization.
-ftree-reassoc
-fno-tree-reassoc
Enable or disable the reassociation of arithmetic expressions on the intermediate representation tree. This optimization rearranges expressions to facilitate other optimizations, such as constant folding or common subexpression elimination. The default behavior is to enable this optimization.
-ftree-scev-cprop
-fno-tree-scev-cprop
This option enables or disables the optimization that performs constant propagation on loop-invariant values derived from the Scalar Evolution analysis. This can improve performance by replacing loop-invariant expressions with their computed constant values. The default behavior is to apply this optimization.
-ftree-schedule
-fno-tree-schedule
Enable or disable instruction scheduling on the intermediate representation tree. Instruction scheduling reorders instructions to improve instruction-level parallelism and hide latencies, potentially improving performance. The default behavior is to enable instruction scheduling.
-ftree-slp-vectorize
-fno-tree-slp-vectorize
This option enables or disables Statement-Level Parallelism (SLP) vectorization on the intermediate representation tree. SLP vectorization identifies sequences of independent operations that can be performed in parallel using SIMD instructions. The default behavior is to apply this optimization.
-ftree-sra
-fno-tree-sra
Enable or disable the stack register allocation optimization on the intermediate representation tree. This optimization attempts to allocate registers from the stack, which can improve performance by reducing memory access. The default behavior is to enable this optimization.
-ftree-terse-statnums
-fno-tree-terse-statnums
This option enables or disables the use of terse statistics numbers in the tree representation. This can reduce the size of compiler output and improve readability. The default behavior is to use terse statistics numbers.
-ftree-vectorize
-fno-tree-vectorize
This option enables or disables automatic vectorization of loops on the intermediate representation tree. Vectorization transforms loops to operate on multiple data elements simultaneously using SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) instructions, potentially improving performance significantly. The default behavior is to apply loop vectorization.
-ftoplevel-namespaces
-fno-toplevel-namespaces
This option controls whether top-level namespaces are generated. When enabled, the compiler generates separate namespaces for top-level declarations, which can help to avoid name collisions in large projects. The default behavior is to not generate top-level namespaces.
-funsigned-bitfields
This option specifies that bit-fields should be unsigned by default. This is the default behavior. See "-fsigned-bitfields" for more information.
-funsigned-char
This option specifies that `char' is unsigned. The default is implementation-defined. See "-fsigned-char" for more information.
-fvariable-expansion-in-unroller
-fno-variable-expansion-in-unroller
This option enables or disables the expansion of variables in the loop unroller. This optimization can improve performance by allowing the unroller to make more effective use of registers and other resources. The default behavior is to expand variables.
-fverbose-asm
-fno-verbose-asm
This option controls whether the assembler output includes verbose comments. When enabled, the assembler output includes comments that explain the purpose of each instruction and directive. This can be helpful for debugging and understanding the generated code. The default behavior is to not include verbose comments.
-fvect-cost-model=MODEL
This option specifies the cost model to use for vectorization. MODEL may be unlimited, predictive, or dynamic.

"unlimited": Assumes that all vector operations are free. This is the fastest but least accurate model.

"predictive": Estimates the cost of vector operations based on hardware characteristics. This is the default model.

"dynamic": Uses runtime profiling to determine the cost of vector operations. This is the most accurate model, but also the slowest.

-fvisibility=VISIBILITY
Set the default symbol visibility to VISIBILITY. The possible values are "default", "internal", "hidden", and "protected".

This option affects the visibility of symbols (functions and variables) that are not explicitly declared with visibility attributes. The default symbol visibility is "default", which means that symbols are visible both inside and outside the shared object.

"internal": Symbols are visible only within the shared object. This is the most restrictive visibility level.

"hidden": Symbols are visible only within the shared object. This is similar to "internal", but it also prevents symbols from being overridden by symbols in other shared objects.

"protected": Symbols are visible both inside and outside the shared object, but they cannot be overridden by symbols in other shared objects.

-fvolatile-load-store-common
-fno-volatile-load-store-common
This option enables or disables the optimization of volatile load and store operations. When enabled, the compiler treats volatile load and store operations as common, meaning that redundant loads and stores may be eliminated. This can improve performance, but may lead to incorrect behavior if volatile operations are used for synchronization purposes. The default behavior is to not optimize volatile load and store operations.

Note: For example, targets with memory-mapped peripheral registers might require all such accesses to be 16 bits wide; with this flag you can declare all peripheral bit-fields as "unsigned short" (assuming short is 16 bits on these targets) to force GCC to use 16-bit accesses instead of, perhaps, a more efficient 32-bit access.

If this option is disabled, the compiler uses the most efficient instruction. In the previous example, that might be a 32-bit load instruction, even though that accesses bytes that do not contain any portion of the bit-field, or memory-mapped registers unrelated to the one being updated.

In some cases, such as when the "packed" attribute is applied to a structure field, it may not be possible to access the field with a single read or write that is correctly aligned for the target machine. In this case GCC falls back to generating multiple accesses rather than code that will fault or truncate the result at run time.

Note: Due to restrictions of the C/C++11 memory model, write accesses are not allowed to touch non bit-field members. It is therefore recommended to define all bits of the field's type as bit-field members.

The default value of this option is determined by the application binary interface for the target processor.

-fsync-libcalls
-fno-sync-libcalls
This option controls whether any out-of-line instance of the "__sync" family of functions may be used to implement the C++11 "__atomic" family of functions.

The default value of this option is enabled, thus the only useful form of the option is -fno-sync-libcalls. This option is used in the implementation of the libatomic runtime library.

GCC Developer Options

This section describes command-line options that are primarily of interest to GCC developers, including options to support compiler testing and investigation of compiler bugs and compile-time performance problems. This includes options that produce debug dumps at various points in the compilation; that print statistics such as memory use and execution time; and that print information about GCC's configuration, such as where it searches for libraries. You should rarely need to use any of these options for ordinary compilation and linking tasks.

Many developer options that cause GCC to dump output to a file take an optional =filename suffix. You can specify stdout or - to dump to standard output, and stderr for standard error.

If =filename is omitted, a default dump file name is constructed by concatenating the base dump file name, a pass number, phase letter, and pass name. The base dump file name is the name of output file produced by the compiler if explicitly specified and not an executable; otherwise it is the source file name. The pass number is determined by the order passes are registered with the compiler's pass manager. This is generally the same as the order of execution, but passes registered by plugins, target-specific passes, or passes that are otherwise registered late are numbered higher than the pass named final, even if they are executed earlier. The phase letter is one of i (inter-procedural analysis), l (language-specific), r (RTL), or t (tree). The files are created in the directory of the output file.

-fcallgraph-info
-fcallgraph-info=MARKERS
Makes the compiler output callgraph information for the program, on a per-object-file basis. The information is generated in the common VCG format. It can be decorated with additional, per-node and/or per-edge information, if a list of comma-separated markers is additionally specified. When the "su" marker is specified, the callgraph is decorated with stack usage information; it is equivalent to -fstack-usage. When the "da" marker is specified, the callgraph is decorated with information about dynamically allocated objects.

When compiling with -flto, no callgraph information is output along with the object file. At LTO link time, -fcallgraph-info may generate multiple callgraph information files next to intermediate LTO output files.

-dletters
-fdump-rtl-pass
-fdump-rtl-pass=filename
Says to make debugging dumps during compilation at times specified by letters. This is used for debugging the RTL-based passes of the compiler.

Some -dletters switches have different meaning when -E is used for preprocessing.

Debug dumps can be enabled with a -fdump-rtl switch or some -d option letters. Here are the possible letters for use in pass and letters, and their meanings:

-fdump-rtl-alignments
Dump after branch alignments have been computed.
-fdump-rtl-asmcons
Dump after fixing rtl statements that have unsatisfied in/out constraints.
-fdump-rtl-auto_inc_dec
Dump after auto-inc-dec discovery. This pass is only run on architectures that have auto inc or auto dec instructions.
-fdump-rtl-barriers
Dump after cleaning up the barrier instructions.
-fdump-rtl-bbpart
Dump after partitioning hot and cold basic blocks.
-fdump-rtl-bbro
Dump after block reordering.
-fdump-rtl-btl1
-fdump-rtl-btl2
-fdump-rtl-btl1 and -fdump-rtl-btl2 enable dumping after the two branch target load optimization passes.
-fdump-rtl-bypass
Dump after jump bypassing and control flow optimizations.
-fdump-rtl-combine
Dump after the RTL instruction combination pass.
-fdump-rtl-compgotos
Dump after duplicating the computed gotos.
-fdump-rtl-ce1
-fdump-rtl-ce2
-fdump-rtl-ce3
-fdump-rtl-ce1, -fdump-rtl-ce2, and -fdump-rtl-ce3 enable dumping after the three if conversion passes.
-fdump-rtl-cprop_hardreg
Dump after hard register copy propagation.
-fdump-rtl-csa
Dump after combining stack adjustments.
-fdump-rtl-cse1
-fdump-rtl-cse2
-fdump-rtl-cse1 and -fdump-rtl-cse2 enable dumping after the two common subexpression elimination passes.
-fdump-rtl-dce
Dump after the standalone dead code elimination passes.
-fdump-rtl-dbr
Dump after delayed branch scheduling.
-fdump-rtl-dce1
-fdump-rtl-dce2
-fdump-rtl-dce1 and -fdump-rtl-dce2 enable dumping after the two dead store elimination passes.
-fdump-rtl-eh
Dump after finalization of EH handling code.
-fdump-rtl-eh_ranges
Dump after conversion of EH handling range regions.
-fdump-rtl-expand
Dump after RTL generation.
-fdump-rtl-fwprop1
-fdump-rtl-fwprop2
-fdump-rtl-fwprop1 and -fdump-rtl-fwprop2 enable dumping after the two forward propagation passes.
-fdump-rtl-gcse1
-fdump-rtl-gcse2
-fdump-rtl-gcse1 and -fdump-rtl-gcse2 enable dumping after global common subexpression elimination.
-fdump-rtl-init-regs
Dump after the initialization of the registers.
-fdump-rtl-initvals
Dump after the computation of the initial value sets.
-fdump-rtl-into_cfglayout
Dump after converting to cfglayout mode.
-fdump-rtl-ira
Dump after iterated register allocation.
-fdump-rtl-jump
Dump after the second jump optimization.
-fdump-rtl-loop2
-fdump-rtl-loop2 enables dumping after the rtl loop optimization passes.
-fdump-rtl-mach
Dump after performing the machine dependent reorganization pass, if that pass exists.
-fdump-rtl-mode_sw
Dump after removing redundant mode switches.
-fdump-rtl-rnreg
Dump after register renumbering.
-fdump-rtl-roots
Dump after the RTL generation passes.
-fdump-rtl-rrdef
Dump after the instruction grouping pass.
-fdump-rtl-sched-prefer-nonraw-bb
Dump after reordering basic blocks to minimize register pressure.
-fdump-rtl-sched-start
Dump after the instruction scheduler has started.
-fdump-rtl-sel-sched
Dump after the selective scheduler has run.
-fdump-rtl-set-irix-ivs
Dump after the IRIX-style loop invariant value substitution pass.
-fdump-rtl-sink-exp
Dump after the expression sinking pass.
-fdump-rtl-stack-usage
Dump after the stack usage analysis pass.
-fdump-rtl-subreg-names
Dump after adding names to subregister variables.
-fdump-rtl-tail-call
Dump after the tail call optimization pass.
-fdump-rtl-tiv
Dump after the transformation of loop-invariant values.
-fdump-rtl-tmaps
Dump after the loop mapping pass.
-fdump-rtl-trg-insns
Dump after the targeted instructions pass.
-fdump-rtl-tree-ssa
Dump after the conversion of the tree SSA to RTL.
-fdump-rtl-unconst
Dump after the unconst pass.
-fdump-rtl-uninit
Dump after the uninitialized variable detection pass.
-fdump-rtl-verifymode
Dump after setting up verify mode.
-fdump-rtl-vrp
Dump after the value range propagation pass.
-fdump-rtl-zbb
Dump after zero-bounded basic blocks optimization.
-fdump-tree-pass
-fdump-tree-pass=filename
Say to make debugging dumps during compilation at times specified by pass. This is used for debugging the tree-based passes of the compiler.

Debug dumps can be enabled with a -fdump-tree switch or some -d option letters. Here are the possible letters for use in pass and letters, and their meanings:

-fdump-tree-alias
Dump after alias analysis.
-fdump-tree-all
Dump after all passes.
-fdump-tree-asm-common
Dump after lowering to asm_common.
-fdump-tree-bind-elim
Dump after binding elimination.
-fdump-tree-bit-width
Dump after bit-width optimization.
-fdump-tree-bpr
Dump after basic-block reordering.
-fdump-tree-ccp
Dump after constant propagation.
-fdump-tree-chase-for-loop
Dump after loop chase optimization.
-fdump-tree-chase-goto
Dump after goto chase optimization.
-fdump-tree-chase-if-goto
Dump after if-goto chase optimization.
-fdump-tree-chase-if-return
Dump after if-return chase optimization.
-fdump-tree-chase-loop
Dump after loop chase optimization.
-fdump-tree-chase-return
Dump after return chase optimization.
-fdump-tree-chase-switch
Dump after switch chase optimization.
-fdump-tree-coalesce-inlines
Dump after coalescing inlines.
-fdump-tree-copy-propagate
Dump after copy propagation.
-fdump-tree-cprop
Dump after constant property propagation.
-fdump-tree-dce
Dump after dead code elimination.
-fdump-tree-dom-inliner
Dump after dominator-based inlining.
-fdump-tree-for-if
Dump after transforming for loops into if statements.
-fdump-tree-fre
Dump after full redundant expression elimination.
-fdump-tree-graph-pool
Dump after graph pool allocation.
-fdump-tree-if-conversion
Dump after if conversion.
-fdump-tree-inliner
Dump after inlining.
-fdump-tree-isolate-paths
Dump after isolating paths.
-fdump-tree-ivopts
Dump after loop invariant optimization.
-fdump-tree-loop-distribute
Dump after loop distribution.
-fdump-tree-loop-if-convert
Dump after loop if conversion.
-fdump-tree-loop-load-store-extend
Dump after loop load/store extension.
-fdump-tree-loop-optimize
Dump after loop optimizations.
-fdump-tree-loop-vectorize
Dump after loop vectorization.
-fdump-tree-lse
Dump after local scalar evolution.
-fdump-tree-live-range-split
Dump after live range splitting.
-fdump-tree-me
Dump after machine epsilon propagation.
-fdump-tree-nongcc-loops
Dump after non-GCC loops optimization.
-fdump-tree-optimize
Dump after optimization passes.
-fdump-tree-partial-inliner
Dump after partial inlining.
-fdump-tree-pe
Dump after promotion of expression.
-fdump-tree-phiprop
Dump after PHI propagation.
-fdump-tree-pre
Dump after premature expression elimination.
-fdump-tree-pta
Dump after pointer type aliasing analysis.
-fdump-tree-reassoc
Dump after reassociation.
-fdump-tree-scev-cprop
Dump after scalar evolution based constant propagation.
-fdump-tree-schedule
Dump after instruction scheduling.
-fdump-tree-slp-vectorize
Dump after SLP vectorization.
-fdump-tree-sra
Dump after stack register allocation.
-fdump-tree-terse-statnums
Dump using terse statistics numbers.
-fdump-tree-uninit
Dump after uninitialized variable detection.
-fdump-tree-vectorize
Dump after vectorization.
-fdump-tree-vrp
Dump after value range propagation.
-fdump-rtl-outof_cfglayout
Volcar después de la conversión desde el modo cfglayout.
-fdump-rtl-peephole2
Volcar después del pase peephole.
-fdump-rtl-postreload
Volcar después de las optimizaciones post-reload.
-fdump-rtl-pro_and_epilogue
Volcar después de generar los prólogos y epílogos de la función.
-fdump-rtl-sched1
-fdump-rtl-sched2
-fdump-rtl-sched1 y -fdump-rtl-sched2 habilitan la salida después de los pases de planificación de bloques básicos.
-fdump-rtl-ree
Volcar después de la eliminación de extensión con signo/cero.
-fdump-rtl-seqabstr
Volcar después del descubrimiento de secuencias comunes.
-fdump-rtl-shorten
Volcar después de acortar saltos.
-fdump-rtl-sibling
Volcar después de las optimizaciones de llamadas de hermanos.
-fdump-rtl-split1
-fdump-rtl-split2
-fdump-rtl-split3
-fdump-rtl-split4
-fdump-rtl-split5
Estas opciones habilitan la salida después de cinco rondas de división de instrucciones.
-fdump-rtl-sms
Volcar después de la planificación de módulos. Este pase solo se ejecuta en algunas arquitecturas.
-fdump-rtl-stack
Volcar después de la conversión de registros de GCC de "archivo de registros plano" a los registros similares a pila de x87. Este pase solo se ejecuta en variantes x86.
-fdump-rtl-subreg1
-fdump-rtl-subreg2
-fdump-rtl-subreg1 y -fdump-rtl-subreg2 habilitan la salida después de los dos pases de expansión de subregistros.
-fdump-rtl-unshare
Volcar después de que todo el RTL se haya desvinculado.
-fdump-rtl-vartrack
Volcar después del seguimiento de variables.
-fdump-rtl-vregs
Volcar después de la conversión de registros virtuales a registros físicos.
-fdump-rtl-web
Volcar después de la división de rangos de vida.
-fdump-rtl-regclass
-fdump-rtl-subregs_of_mode_init
-fdump-rtl-subregs_of_mode_finish
-fdump-rtl-dfinit
-fdump-rtl-dfinish
Estos volcados están definidos pero siempre producen archivos vacíos.
-da
-fdump-rtl-all
Produce todos los volcados listados anteriormente.
-dA
Anota la salida del ensamblador con información de depuración miscelánea.
-dD
Volcar todas las definiciones de macros, al final del preprocesamiento, además de la salida normal.
-dH
Produce un volcado de núcleo cada vez que ocurre un error.
-dp
Anota la salida del ensamblador con un comentario indicando qué patrón y alternativa se utilizan. También se imprime la longitud y el costo de cada instrucción.
-dP
Volcar el RTL en la salida del ensamblador como un comentario antes de cada instrucción. También activa la anotación -dp.
-dx
Solo genera RTL para una función en lugar de compilarla. Generalmente se usa con -fdump-rtl-expand.
-fdump-debug
Volcar información de depuración generada durante la fase de generación de depuración.
-fdump-earlydebug
Volcar información de depuración generada durante la fase temprana de generación de depuración.
-fdump-noaddr
Al realizar volcados de depuración, suprima la salida de direcciones. Esto hace que sea más factible usar diff en los volcados de depuración para invocaciones del compilador con binarios de compilador diferentes y/o diferentes ubicaciones de inicio de texto / bss / data / heap / stack / dso.
-freport-bug
Recopila y vierte información de depuración en un archivo temporal si ocurre un error interno del compilador (ICE).
-fdump-unnumbered
Al realizar volcados de depuración, suprima los números de instrucción y la salida de direcciones. Esto hace que sea más factible usar diff en los volcados de depuración para invocaciones del compilador con diferentes opciones, en particular con y sin -g.
-fdump-unnumbered-links
Al realizar volcados de depuración (ver opción -d anterior), suprima los números de instrucción para los enlaces a las instrucciones anterior y siguiente en una secuencia.
-fdump-ipa-switch
-fdump-ipa-switch-options
Controla el volcado en varias etapas del árbol del lenguaje de análisis interprocedural a un archivo. El nombre del archivo se genera agregando un sufijo específico del switch al nombre del archivo fuente, y el archivo se crea en el mismo directorio que el archivo de salida. Los siguientes volcados son posibles:
all
Habilita todos los volcados de análisis interprocedural.
cgraph
Vierte información sobre la optimización del grafo de llamadas, la eliminación de funciones no utilizadas y las decisiones de inlineado.
inline
Volcar después del inlineado de funciones.
strubm
Volcar después de seleccionar modos "strub", y registrar las selecciones como atributos de función.
strub
Transformaciones de volcado "strub": cambios de interfaz, envoltura de funciones e inserción de llamadas a builtins para limpieza de pila y marcas de agua.

Adicionalmente, se pueden proporcionar las opciones -optimized, -missed, -note y -all, con el mismo significado que para -fopt-info, por defecto -optimized.

Por ejemplo, -fdump-ipa-inline-optimized-missed emitirá información sobre sitios de llamada que fueron inlineados, junto con sitios de llamada que no fueron inlineados.

Por defecto, el volcado contendrá mensajes sobre optimizaciones exitosas (equivalente a -optimized) junto con detalles de bajo nivel sobre el análisis.

-fdump-lang
Volcar información específica del lenguaje. El nombre del archivo se crea agregando .lang al nombre del archivo fuente.
-fdump-lang-all
-fdump-lang-switch
-fdump-lang-switch-options
-fdump-lang-switch-options=filename
Controla el volcado de información específica del lenguaje. Las porciones de options y filename se comportan como se describe en la opción -fdump-tree. Se aceptan los siguientes valores de switch:
all
Habilita todos los volcados específicos del lenguaje.
class
Volcar información de la jerarquía de clases. La información de tablas virtuales se emite a menos que se especifique 'slim'. Esta opción es aplicable solo a C++.
module
Volcar información de módulos. Las opciones lineno (ubicaciones), graph (alcanzabilidad), blocks (agrupaciones), uid (serialización), alias (fusionable), asmname (Elrond), eh (mapeador) y vops (macros) pueden proporcionar información adicional. Esta opción es aplicable solo a C++.
raw
Volcar los datos brutos del árbol interno. Esta opción es aplicable solo a C++.
-fdump-passes
Imprime en stderr la lista de pases de optimización que están activados y desactivados por las opciones actuales de la línea de comandos.
-fdump-statistics-option
Habilita y controla el volcado de estadísticas de pases en un archivo separado. El nombre del archivo se genera agregando un sufijo que termina en .statistics al nombre del archivo fuente, y el archivo se crea en el mismo directorio que el archivo de salida. Si se utiliza la forma -option, -stats hace que los contadores se sumen en toda la unidad de compilación mientras que -details vierte cada evento a medida que los pases los generan. Por defecto, sin ninguna opción, se suman los contadores para cada función compilada.
-fdump-tree-all
-fdump-tree-switch
-fdump-tree-switch-options
-fdump-tree-switch-options=filename
Control the dumping at various stages of processing the intermediate language tree to a file. If the -options form is used, options is a list of - separated options which control the details of the dump. Not all options are applicable to all dumps; those that are not meaningful are ignored. The following options are available
address
Print the address of each node. Usually this is not meaningful as it changes according to the environment and source file. Its primary use is for tying up a dump file with a debug environment.
asmname
If "DECL_ASSEMBLER_NAME" has been set for a given decl, use that in the dump instead of "DECL_NAME". Its primary use is ease of use working backward from mangled names in the assembly file.
slim
When dumping front-end intermediate representations, inhibit dumping of members of a scope or body of a function merely because that scope has been reached. Only dump such items when they are directly reachable by some other path.

When dumping pretty-printed trees, this option inhibits dumping the bodies of control structures.

When dumping RTL, print the RTL in slim (condensed) form instead of the default LISP-like representation.

raw
Print a raw representation of the tree. By default, trees are pretty-printed into a C-like representation.
details
Enable more detailed dumps (not honored by every dump option). Also include information from the optimization passes.
stats
Enable dumping various statistics about the pass (not honored by every dump option).
blocks
Enable showing basic block boundaries (disabled in raw dumps).
graph
For each of the other indicated dump files (-fdump-rtl-pass), dump a representation of the control flow graph suitable for viewing with GraphViz to file.passid.pass.dot. Each function in the file is pretty-printed as a subgraph, so that GraphViz can render them all in a single plot.

This option currently only works for RTL dumps, and the RTL is always dumped in slim form.

vops
Enable showing virtual operands for every statement.
lineno
Enable showing line numbers for statements.
uid
Enable showing the unique ID ("DECL_UID") for each variable.
verbose
Enable showing the tree dump for each statement.
eh
Enable showing the EH region number holding each statement.
scev
Enable showing scalar evolution analysis details.
optimized
Enable showing optimization information (only available in certain passes).
missed
Enable showing missed optimization information (only available in certain passes).
note
Enable other detailed optimization information (only available in certain passes).
all
Turn on all options, except raw, slim, verbose and lineno.
optall
Turn on all optimization options, i.e., optimized, missed, and note.

To determine what tree dumps are available or find the dump for a pass of interest follow the steps below.

1.
Invoke GCC with -fdump-passes and in the stderr output look for a code that corresponds to the pass you are interested in. For example, the codes "tree-evrp", "tree-vrp1", and "tree-vrp2" correspond to the three Value Range Propagation passes. The number at the end distinguishes distinct invocations of the same pass.
2.
To enable the creation of the dump file, append the pass code to the -fdump- option prefix and invoke GCC with it. For example, to enable the dump from the Early Value Range Propagation pass, invoke GCC with the -fdump-tree-evrp option. Optionally, you may specify the name of the dump file. If you don't specify one, GCC creates as described below.
3.
Find the pass dump in a file whose name is composed of three components separated by a period: the name of the source file GCC was invoked to compile, a numeric suffix indicating the pass number followed by the letter t for tree passes (and the letter r for RTL passes), and finally the pass code. For example, the Early VRP pass dump might be in a file named myfile.c.038t.evrp in the current working directory. Note that the numeric codes are not stable and may change from one version of GCC to another.
-fopt-info
-fopt-info-options
-fopt-info-options=filename
Controls optimization dumps from various optimization passes. If the -options form is used, options is a list of - separated option keywords to select the dump details and optimizations.

The options can be divided into three groups:

1.
options describing what kinds of messages should be emitted,
2.
options describing the verbosity of the dump, and
3.
options describing which optimizations should be included.

The options from each group can be freely mixed as they are non-overlapping. However, in case of any conflicts, the later options override the earlier options on the command line.

The following options control which kinds of messages should be emitted:

optimized
Print information when an optimization is successfully applied. It is up to a pass to decide which information is relevant. For example, the vectorizer passes print the source location of loops which are successfully vectorized.
missed
Print information about missed optimizations. Individual passes control which information to include in the output.
note
Print verbose information about optimizations, such as certain transformations, more detailed messages about decisions etc.
all
Print detailed optimization information. This includes optimized, missed, and note.

The following option controls the dump verbosity:

internals
By default, only "high-level" messages are emitted. This option enables additional, more detailed, messages, which are likely to only be of interest to GCC developers.

One or more of the following option keywords can be used to describe a group of optimizations:

ipa
Enable dumps from all interprocedural optimizations.
loop
Enable dumps from all loop optimizations.
inline
Enable dumps from all inlining optimizations.
omp
Enable dumps from all OMP (Offloading and Multi Processing) optimizations.
vec
Enable dumps from all vectorization optimizations.
optall
Enable dumps from all optimizations. This is a superset of the optimization groups listed above.

If options is omitted, it defaults to optimized-optall, which means to dump messages about successful optimizations from all the passes, omitting messages that are treated as "internals".

If the filename is provided, then the dumps from all the applicable optimizations are concatenated into the filename. Otherwise the dump is output onto stderr. Though multiple -fopt-info options are accepted, only one of them can include a filename. If other filenames are provided then all but the first such option are ignored.

Note that the output filename is overwritten in case of multiple translation units. If a combined output from multiple translation units is desired, stderr should be used instead.

In the following example, the optimization info is output to stderr:

gcc -O3 -fopt-info

This example:

gcc -O3 -fopt-info-missed=missed.all

outputs missed optimization report from all the passes into missed.all, and this one:

gcc -O2 -ftree-vectorize -fopt-info-vec-missed

prints information about missed optimization opportunities from vectorization passes on stderr. Note that -fopt-info-vec-missed is equivalent to -fopt-info-missed-vec. The order of the optimization group names and message types listed after -fopt-info does not matter.

>Como otro ejemplo, 

gcc -O3 -fopt-info-inline-optimized-missed=inline.txt

genera información sobre optimizaciones fallidas, así como ubicaciones optimizadas de todos los pases de inlining en inline.txt.

Finalmente, considera:

gcc -fopt-info-vec-missed=vec.miss -fopt-info-loop-optimized=loop.opt

Aquí los dos nombres de archivo de salida vec.miss y loop.opt están en conflicto, ya que solo se permite un archivo de salida. En este caso, solo se aplica la primera opción y las subsiguientes se ignoran. Por lo tanto, solo se produce vec.miss, que contiene volcados del vectorizador sobre oportunidades perdidas.

-fsave-optimization-record
Escribe un archivo SRCFILE.opt-record.json.gz detallando qué optimizaciones se realizaron, para aquellas optimizaciones que soportan -fopt-info.

Esta opción es experimental y el formato de los datos dentro del archivo JSON comprimido está sujeto a cambios.

Es aproximadamente equivalente a una versión legible por máquina de -fopt-info-all, como una colección de mensajes con archivo fuente, número de línea y número de columna, con los siguientes datos adicionales para cada mensaje:

  • el recuento de ejecución del código que se está optimizando, junto con metadatos sobre si provino de datos de perfil reales o solo de una estimación, lo que permite a los consumidores priorizar los mensajes por la "calidez" del código,
  • el nombre de la función del código que se está optimizando, cuando sea aplicable,
  • la "cadena de inlining" para el código que se está optimizando, de modo que cuando una función se inlinea en varios lugares diferentes (que a su vez pueden ser inlineados), el lector pueda distinguir entre las copias,
  • objetos que identifican aquellas partes del mensaje que se refieren a expresiones, declaraciones o nodos de la tabla de símbolos, de qué categoría son y, cuando estén disponibles, su ubicación en el código fuente,
  • el pase de GCC que emitió el mensaje, y
  • la ubicación en el propio código de GCC desde donde se emitió el mensaje

Además, algunos mensajes están lógicamente anidados dentro de otros mensajes, lo que refleja detalles de implementación de los pases de optimización.

-fsched-verbose=n
En objetivos que utilizan programación de instrucciones, esta opción controla la cantidad de salida de depuración que el programador imprime en los archivos de volcado.

Para n mayor que cero, -fsched-verbose genera la misma información que -fdump-rtl-sched1 y -fdump-rtl-sched2. Para n mayor que uno, también genera probabilidades de bloque básico, información detallada de la lista de preparación e información de unidad/insn. Para n mayor que dos, incluye RTL en el punto de aborto, información de flujo de control y regiones. Y para n mayor que cuatro, -fsched-verbose también incluye información de dependencia.

-fenable-kind-pass
-fdisable-kind-pass=range-list
Este es un conjunto de opciones que se utilizan para deshabilitar/habilitar explícitamente pases de optimización. Estas opciones están destinadas a la depuración de GCC. Los usuarios del compilador deben usar opciones regulares para habilitar/deshabilitar pases en su lugar.
-fdisable-ipa-pass
Deshabilita el pase IPA pass. pass es el nombre del pase. Si el mismo pase se invoca estáticamente en el compilador varias veces, el nombre del pase debe ir seguido de un número secuencial comenzando desde 1.
-fdisable-rtl-pass
-fdisable-rtl-pass=range-list
Deshabilita el pase RTL pass. pass es el nombre del pase. Si el mismo pase se invoca estáticamente en el compilador varias veces, el nombre del pase debe ir seguido de un número secuencial comenzando desde 1. range-list es una lista separada por comas de rangos de funciones o nombres de ensamblador. Cada rango es un par de números separados por dos puntos. El rango es inclusivo en ambos extremos. Si el rango es trivial, el par de números se puede simplificar como un solo número.
